course.name: Islamic Humanities
course.tagline: Map game, timeline, key figures and their works.

cards.simple: The community of Muslim believers as a whole, across tribe, ethnicity and place.
more: The Qur’an uses umma for a people with a shared religious calling. After the hijra (622) it came to mean the new community at Medina, bound by faith rather than by kinship, which was a sharp break with tribal Arabia. The early agreement known as the “Constitution of Medina” also brought allied Jewish clans within its terms of mutual defence.

Common confusion: the umma is a religious community, not a state. It has been ruled by caliphs, by many rival dynasties at once and today by dozens of nation-states. Modern movements from pan-Islamism to the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (founded 1969) appeal to it as a transnational ideal.
It is also not an Arab community: most Muslims today are not Arabs, and a majority live in the Asia-Pacific region.
cards.example: Indonesia has the largest Muslim population of any country. Its pilgrims at the hajj in Mecca, praying alongside Nigerians, Turks and Bosnians, are the umma made visible.
cards.numbersSource: Pew Research Center, “How the Global Religious Landscape Changed From 2010 to 2020” (2025); Pew, “Mapping the Global Muslim Population” (2009) for the Shi‘i range.
played: 622: the hijra founds a community at Medina defined by faith, not tribe.
632: Muhammad dies, and the umma must decide who leads it (the caliphate).
From the 10th century: one umma, many rulers. Rival caliphs and sultans govern, but scholars, pilgrims and trade keep a shared religious world.
Today: about a quarter of humanity, in dozens of states, still spoken of as one umma.

cards.simple: Muhammad’s emigration from Mecca to Medina in 622, which founded the first Muslim community-state and marks year 1 of the Islamic (AH) calendar.
more: After years of opposition from the leaders of Quraysh in Mecca, Muhammad accepted an invitation from the tribes of Yathrib, which became Madinat al-Nabi, “the city of the Prophet”. The emigrants (muhajirun) and the Medinan helpers (ansar) formed one community under his leadership.

The Islamic calendar, traditionally instituted under the caliph ‘Umar, counts years from the start of the year of the hijra (AH = anno Hegirae). Its year is twelve lunar months, so it runs about 11 days shorter than the solar year and Ramadan moves through the seasons.
Common confusion: the calendar does not start at Muhammad’s birth (traditionally 570) or the first revelation (610), but at the founding of the community.
cards.example: The Prophet’s Mosque in Medina began as the courtyard of Muhammad’s house after the hijra, the model for later congregational mosques.
played: 610: the first revelation, in Mecca (traditionally on Mount Hira).
622: the hijra to Medina; year 1 AH.
630: Mecca submits to Muhammad without major bloodshed.
632: Muhammad dies in Medina, now head of much of Arabia.

cards.simple: The scripture of Islam, 114 suras (chapters) in Arabic, which Muslims believe is God’s word revealed to Muhammad between about 610 and 632.
more: The suras are arranged roughly from longest to shortest after the short opening sura, al-Fatiha, not in the order of revelation. Scholars group them as Meccan (shorter, on God, judgement and prophecy) and Medinan (longer, including community law).

Muslim tradition holds that the text was gathered after Muhammad’s death and fixed in a standard codex under the caliph ‘Uthman (r. 644–656). Muslims regard the Arabic text as inimitable (i‘jaz), so translations are treated as interpretations. Its literary Arabic became the reference standard for the language and for later literature.
Common confusion: the Qur’an is not the hadith. The Qur’an is held to be God’s speech; hadith are reports about what the Prophet said and did.
cards.example: Al-Fatiha (7 verses) is recited in every unit (rak‘a) of the daily prayer, so a Muslim who prays recites it at least 17 times a day.
cards.numbersSource: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Qur’an”; verse total by the Kufan count used in the standard Cairo edition (other early counts differ slightly).
played: c. 610–632: revealed piecemeal, recited and memorized.
After 632: collected into written form (tradition credits Abu Bakr and Zayd ibn Thabit).
‘Uthman (r. 644–656): a standard codex is copied and sent to the main cities.
1924: the Cairo printed edition becomes the most widely used text today.

cards.simple: Hadith are reports, each carried by a chain of transmitters (isnad), of what Muhammad said, did or approved, and they are the main evidence for his sunna, the normative example Muslims follow.
more: Sunna is the model; hadith are the evidence for it. Scholars judged a report mainly by its chain: were the transmitters reliable, and could they have met? Reports were graded sahih (sound), hasan (good) or da‘if (weak).

Sunnis give special authority to six 9th-century collections, above all those of al-Bukhari (d. 870) and Muslim (d. 875). Shi‘is rely on their own collections, such as al-Kulayni’s al-Kafi, which also include the sayings of the Imams.
Common confusion: a hadith is not part of the Qur’an, and “sunna” here is not the same word as “Sunni”, though Sunnis take their name from it (ahl al-sunna, “people of the sunna”).
cards.example: The “Hadith of Gabriel” in Muslim’s Sahih: a stranger questions the Prophet about islam, iman (faith) and ihsan (excellence), then is identified as the angel Gabriel.
played: A Companion sees or hears the Prophet and reports it.
Successive transmitters pass it on: “A told me that B said that…”.
A 9th-century compiler checks each link and grades the chain.
Jurists then use a sound hadith as the second source of law after the Qur’an.

cards.simple: Shahada (profession of faith), salat (prayer five times a day), zakat (obligatory alms), sawm (fasting in Ramadan), hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca, once if able).
more: The pillars are acts, not beliefs: the shared ritual core that makes Muslims across schools and sects recognizable to one another. Sunnis and Shi‘is perform all five, though Shi‘i theology classifies the obligations in its own way and adds others.

Zakat is not voluntary charity (sadaqa) but an obligation, customarily 2.5% of qualifying wealth held for a year. Sawm means no food, drink or sex from dawn to sunset during Ramadan, the ninth lunar month.
Common confusion: the hajj is the pilgrimage in the month of Dhu al-Hijja; a visit to Mecca at other times is the lesser pilgrimage, ‘umra.
cards.example: On 9 Dhu al-Hijja pilgrims stand in prayer on the plain of ‘Arafat; the next day Muslims everywhere celebrate ‘Id al-Adha with a sacrifice.
cards.numbersSource: Saudi General Authority for Statistics (GASTAT), Hajj Statistics 2024; Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Pillars of Islam”.
played: 8 Dhu al-Hijja: pilgrims in ihram (simple white garments, a state of consecration) go to Mina.
9th: standing at ‘Arafat, the heart of the hajj.
10th: stoning of the pillar at Mina, animal sacrifice, cutting the hair.
Circling the Ka‘ba (tawaf) completes the rites.

cards.simple: The caliph (khalifa, “successor”) was the leader of the Muslim community after Muhammad: first the four Rashidun (632–661), then the Umayyad and Abbasid dynasties.
more: A caliph succeeded to Muhammad’s leadership of the community, not to his prophethood: no new revelation. Early caliphs were styled “successor of the Messenger of God”; the Umayyads also used “deputy of God”, a claim to religious authority later scholars resisted.

After the four Rashidun caliphs the office became dynastic: Umayyads, then Abbasids. From the 10th century there were rival caliphs (Fatimids in Cairo, Umayyads in Córdoba). After the Mongols took Baghdad in 1258, the Mamluks kept a line of figurehead Abbasid caliphs in Cairo. The Ottoman caliphate was abolished in 1924.
Common confusion: “caliph” and “sultan” differ. Sultans held military power; caliphs (after c. 945) were often symbols of legitimacy who confirmed them.
cards.example: Abu Bakr, Muhammad’s father-in-law and close Companion, was acclaimed the first caliph at a meeting in Medina (the Saqifa) in 632.
cards.numbersSource: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “caliph” and entries on each caliph.
played: 632: Abu Bakr chosen in Medina.
656: ‘Uthman is killed; ‘Ali’s caliphate is contested in the first civil war (fitna).
661: ‘Ali is assassinated; Mu‘awiya founds the Umayyad dynasty.
1924: the Turkish Republic abolishes the last caliphate.

cards.simple: The split between Sunnis and Shi‘is began as a dispute over who should lead after Muhammad, with Shi‘is (“partisans” of ‘Ali) holding that leadership belonged to ‘Ali and his descendants, the Imams.
more: Sunnis (ahl al-sunna wa-l-jama‘a) accept the first four caliphs, in their historical order, as rightly guided, with leadership resting on the community’s choice. Shi‘is hold that Muhammad designated ‘Ali and that religious authority passed to a line of Imams from his family. Twelvers (the largest Shi‘i branch) believe the twelfth Imam went into hiding in 874 and will return.

Both share the Qur’an, the five pillars and prayer toward Mecca. They differ in hadith collections, schools of law (the Shi‘i Ja‘fari school), some ritual details and religious authority: in modern Twelver Shi‘ism, senior jurists act as guides for believers.
Common confusion: the divide was political before it was theological, and it is not simply Iran vs Arabs: there are large Shi‘i populations in Iraq, Pakistan, India and Lebanon.
cards.example: At Karbala (680) the Prophet’s grandson Husayn and a small band were killed by an Umayyad army. Shi‘is mourn him every year on ‘Ashura, 10 Muharram, and his shrine at Karbala is a major pilgrimage site.
numbers: Shi‘is living in Iran, Pakistan, India, Iraq
cards.numbersSource: Pew Research Center, “Mapping the Global Muslim Population” (2009), estimates given as ranges because sectarian data are sparse; Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Battle of Karbala”.
played: 632: Abu Bakr becomes caliph; ‘Ali’s supporters believe he should have led.
656–661: ‘Ali is caliph amid civil war, then is killed.
680: Husayn is killed at Karbala, giving the movement its martyr.
1501: the Safavids make Twelver Shi‘ism the state religion of Iran.

cards.simple: Sharia is God’s law as an ideal path, while fiqh is the human jurisprudence by which scholars derive concrete rulings from the Qur’an, sunna, consensus (ijma‘) and analogy (qiyas).
more: Sharia is God’s law as an ideal; fiqh is the jurists’ fallible attempt to know it, which is why it is plural (several schools) and can change. The effort of reasoning is ijtihad; following an established school’s rulings is taqlid.
Fiqh sorts every act into five categories: obligatory, recommended, permitted, discouraged and forbidden. Much of it concerns ritual (prayer, fasting, purity), not only crime or the state.
Common confusion: “sharia law” in modern headlines usually means a state’s codified selection of fiqh, something premodern jurists, working through schools and judges, did not have.
cards.example: The Qur’an forbids khamr (wine). By analogy (qiyas), jurists extended the ban to other intoxicants because they share its effective cause, intoxication.
played: Question: is date-wine allowed? No explicit verse names it.
Qur’an: wine is forbidden. Sunna: hadith say “every intoxicant is forbidden”.
Cause (‘illa) of the rule: intoxication. Date-wine intoxicates.
Ruling by analogy: forbidden. Where scholars agree, consensus (ijma‘) settles it.

cards.simple: The ‘ulama’ are the learned scholars of religion and law (jurists, judges, teachers and muftis), who often mediated between rulers and the people.
more: Islam has no ordained clergy or church. Scholarly authority came from learning, certified person to person: a teacher gave a student an ijaza (licence) to transmit a text. Most Sunni scholars belonged to one of four schools of law (madhhabs).

A qadi judges cases in court; a mufti gives non-binding legal opinions (fatwas). Rulers needed the ‘ulama’ for legitimacy and administration; the ‘ulama’ needed patronage, often through waqf endowments.

Common confusion: in Twelver Shi‘ism a hierarchy of senior jurists (mujtahids, the highest a marja‘, “source of emulation”) developed, giving Shi‘i ‘ulama’ more independent authority than most Sunni scholars had.
cards.example: Ebussuud Efendi (d. 1574), chief mufti (şeyhülislam) under Süleyman the Magnificent, issued fatwas reconciling the sultan’s laws with the sharia.
played: A student reads law with a master in a madrasa.
He receives an ijaza, a licence to teach that text.
He is appointed qadi, or teaches and issues fatwas as a mufti.
His rulings join his school’s tradition for later jurists.

cards.simple: A madrasa is a college of religious and legal learning, which spread widely from the 11th century, notably through the Seljuk vizier Nizam al-Mulk’s Nizamiyya colleges.
more: A madrasa taught fiqh above all, with hadith, Qur’an and Arabic, and usually lodged and paid its students. It was funded by a waqf, and its deed often fixed which school of law it served.

Nizam al-Mulk (d. 1092), vizier to the Seljuk sultans, founded madrasas in Baghdad and other cities. They trained Sunni scholars and officials at a time when the Shi‘i Fatimids ruled Egypt. Al-Ghazali taught at the Baghdad Nizamiyya.
Common confusion: a degree came from a teacher’s licence (ijaza), not from the institution. And the madrasa was not the first place of learning: teaching had long happened in mosques.
cards.example: The Sultan Hasan complex in Cairo (1356–1363), built under the Mamluks, places four madrasas, one for each Sunni school of law, around a four-iwan courtyard.
numbers: Al-Azhar, Cairo (mosque, later a centre of learning)
cards.numbersSource: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Niẓāmiyyah”, “al-Azhar University” and “Mosque of Sultan Ḥasan”.
played: A founder endows shops or land as a waqf.
The income builds the madrasa and pays professors (Shafi‘i law at the Baghdad Nizamiyya).
Students live there on stipends and study for years.
Graduates become qadis, teachers and officials across the realm.

cards.simple: A charitable endowment: property whose income is dedicated in perpetuity to a purpose such as a mosque, madrasa, hospital or fountain.
more: The founder gives up ownership; the property can no longer be sold or inherited, and an administrator (mutawalli) under a judge’s supervision spends the income as the deed directs. It was the financial backbone of much of the premodern Islamic world’s education and welfare.
A family waqf could name the founder’s descendants as beneficiaries, which also protected wealth from confiscation and from the fixed shares of inheritance law.

Common confusion: waqf is not zakat. Zakat is an annual obligation on wealth; a waqf is a voluntary, permanent endowment. In the 19th and 20th centuries states took waqfs under ministries, weakening the ‘ulama’s independent income.
cards.example: The Süleymaniye complex in Istanbul ran on waqf income: besides the mosque it endowed madrasas, a hospital, a public kitchen (imaret) and baths.
played: A merchant signs a deed before a qadi dedicating the rents of his shops.
The shops can never again be sold.
The administrator collects the rent and pays teachers and a fountain’s upkeep.
Centuries later, the Ottoman state places waqfs under a ministry (1826).

cards.simple: Dhimmis were protected non-Muslim communities (Jews, Christians and others) under Muslim rule, who kept communal autonomy and paid a poll tax, the jizya.
more: The status rested on the Qur’an’s recognition of “People of the Book” and on surrender treaties made during the conquests; it was later extended to Zoroastrians and others. Dhimmis kept their worship, property and communal law, and paid the jizya in place of military service.

Juristic texts also imposed restrictions (on new church building, dress, bearing arms), often attributed to a “Pact of ‘Umar” whose early date historians doubt. How strictly they were enforced varied greatly by ruler and period.

Common confusion: dhimma was neither modern equality nor constant persecution; it was a protected but subordinate status. For centuries most people in conquered lands like Egypt and Syria were dhimmis.
cards.example: Hasdai ibn Shaprut, a Jewish physician and diplomat, served the Umayyad caliph ‘Abd al-Rahman III in 10th-century Córdoba.
played: 7th century: a city surrenders by treaty; its Christians keep churches and pay tribute.
Jurists systematize the terms: jizya per adult male, communal self-rule.
Ottoman era: communities organized under their own religious heads (the millets).
1856: the Ottoman Reform Edict declares equality and ends the jizya.

cards.simple: In Abbasid Baghdad (8th–10th c.), Greek, Persian and Indian works in philosophy, medicine, mathematics and astronomy were translated into Arabic, often through Syriac.
more: Caliphs, viziers and wealthy patrons paid for translations for practical and prestige reasons: medicine, astronomy for the calendar and astrology, and arguments for theology. Cheap paper, which spread from the mid-8th century, made books far cheaper.

Many translators were Christians, such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq (809–873), who rendered Galen into Syriac and Arabic. The House of Wisdom under al-Ma’mun (r. 813–833) is famous, but historians debate whether it was an academy or mainly a palace library; the movement was broader than one building.
Common confusion: scholars writing in Arabic did not just preserve the Greeks for Europe. They criticized and extended them, and from the 12th century their own works were translated into Latin.
cards.example: Al-Khwarizmi (c. 780–c. 850), working in Baghdad, wrote al-Jabr, which gave us “algebra”; the Latin form of his name gave us “algorithm”.
played: Galen’s medical works, in Greek.
Hunayn’s circle translates them into Syriac and Arabic in 9th-century Baghdad.
Physicians like Ibn Sina (980–1037) build on them in Arabic.
12th century: Gerard of Cremona in Toledo translates Ibn Sina’s Canon into Latin for European medical schools.

cards.simple: Falsafa is philosophy in the Greek tradition (al-Kindi, al-Farabi, Ibn Sina, Ibn Rushd), while kalam is dialectical theology that uses reason to defend revealed doctrine (Mu‘tazilis, Ash‘aris).
more: Both use reason; they differ in starting point. Falsafa starts from demonstrative reason and Greek texts and sees revelation as truth for the many in images. Kalam starts from revelation and uses argument to defend and clarify it.

The Mu‘tazila stressed God’s justice, human free will and the createdness of the Qur’an. The Ash‘aris (after al-Ash‘ari, d. 935/936) stressed God’s omnipotence, holding that God directly creates every event; this became the main Sunni theology alongside the Maturidi school.

Common confusion: al-Ghazali (1058–1111) did not reject reason or logic. His Incoherence of the Philosophers attacked three of their theses as unbelief: the world’s eternity, God’s not knowing particulars, and denial of bodily resurrection. Ibn Rushd (1126–1198) replied with the Incoherence of the Incoherence.
cards.example: In the mihna (from 833) the caliph al-Ma’mun required scholars to affirm the Mu‘tazili doctrine that the Qur’an was created. Ahmad ibn Hanbal refused and was imprisoned; the policy was abandoned c. 848.
played: Ibn Sina (980–1037) builds a great philosophical system in Arabic.
Al-Ghazali’s Incoherence of the Philosophers (c. 1095) attacks its key claims.
Ibn Rushd answers him (c. 1180), defending philosophy as compatible with revelation.
Ibn Rushd’s commentaries on Aristotle shape Latin scholasticism (“Averroes”).

cards.simple: The mystical dimension of Islam: seeking direct experience of God through devotion, remembrance (dhikr) and discipline, often organized in orders (tariqas) around a master.
more: It grew from early ascetics such as Hasan al-Basri (d. 728) and the woman mystic Rabi‘a al-‘Adawiyya (traditionally d. 801), who spoke of loving God for Himself. From the 12th–13th centuries orders formed, each tracing its teaching through a chain of masters (silsila) back to the Prophet.

Al-Ghazali’s Revival of the Religious Sciences helped place a sharia-observant Sufism at the centre of Sunni life. Orders spread Islam in Anatolia, Central and South Asia and Africa, and some became political: the Safavid dynasty began as a Sufi order.

Common confusion: Sufism is not a sect beside Sunni and Shi‘i Islam; Sufis are found in both, and most followed the law. Some reformers since the 18th century have criticized practices such as saint veneration.
cards.example: The Mevlevi order, founded by followers of Rumi (1207–1273) in Konya, performs the sema, the “whirling” ceremony of remembrance.
played: A seeker (murid) takes an oath of allegiance to a shaykh.
He practises the order’s dhikr, often chanting God’s names, and spiritual discipline.
He passes through spiritual stations (maqamat) under guidance.
Authorized in turn, he becomes a link in the silsila.

cards.simple: The first hereditary caliphate, ruled from Damascus, which expanded from Iberia to Central Asia, made Arabic the language of government and built the Dome of the Rock.
more: Founded by Mu‘awiya after ‘Ali’s death, it turned the caliphate into a hereditary monarchy, which critics, Shi‘i and later Sunni alike, condemned. It relied on an Arab military elite; non-Arab converts (mawali) resented unequal treatment, and that resentment fed the Abbasid revolution.

Under ‘Abd al-Malik (r. 685–705) the state switched its records to Arabic, minted new coins bearing only inscriptions, and built the Dome of the Rock. The conquests reached Iberia (711) and Sind and Transoxiana; a raid into Francia was turned back at Tours (732).
Common confusion: the Umayyads of Córdoba are a separate branch: a survivor, ‘Abd al-Rahman I, founded an emirate there in 756, and ‘Abd al-Rahman III declared a rival caliphate in 929.
cards.example: The Great Mosque of Damascus, built under al-Walid I (r. 705–715) on the site of a Byzantine church, with mosaics of trees, rivers and buildings but no human figures.
cards.numbersSource: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Umayyad dynasty” and “Dome of the Rock”.
played: 661: Mu‘awiya takes power, capital Damascus.
680: Husayn is killed at Karbala by an Umayyad army.
691–692: the Dome of the Rock rises in Jerusalem.
750: the Abbasids overthrow the dynasty; 756: a survivor rules in Córdoba.

cards.simple: The dynasty that overthrew the Umayyads in 750, founded Baghdad in 762 and presided over a golden age of learning, though its real power fragmented long before the Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258.
more: The Abbasids claimed descent from al-‘Abbas, Muhammad’s uncle, and rallied Persian converts and supporters of the Prophet’s family under black banners. Once in power they ruled as Sunni caliphs, disappointing many Shi‘i hopes, and adopted Persian court and bureaucratic traditions, led by viziers.

Under Harun al-Rashid (r. 786–809) and al-Ma’mun (r. 813–833) Baghdad became a centre of trade, translation and scholarship. From 945 the Shi‘i Buyids controlled Baghdad, and from 1055 the Seljuk sultans: the caliph kept religious prestige but lost real power.

Common confusion: the “golden age” did not end when the caliphs lost power. Much of the great science and literature came from regional courts (Samanid Bukhara, Buyid Iran, Fatimid Cairo) that nominally deferred to or rivalled Baghdad.
cards.example: Al-Mansur’s Round City of Baghdad (762), with the caliph’s palace and mosque at the centre of concentric walls.
played: 750: the Umayyads are defeated at the Zab; the Abbasids take power.
762: al-Mansur founds Baghdad on the Tigris.
945: the Buyids hold Baghdad; the caliph becomes a figurehead.
1258: the Mongols sack Baghdad and kill the caliph al-Musta‘sim.

cards.simple: Mamluks were slave-soldiers who became rulers, and their sultanate in Egypt and Syria (1250–1517) stopped the Mongols at ‘Ayn Jalut in 1260 before falling to the Ottomans.
more: From the 9th century rulers bought boys from the steppe, mostly Turks, converted and trained them as an elite cavalry loyal to their master. In Egypt the mamluks of the Ayyubid sultan seized power in 1250 and ruled as a self-renewing military caste: new rulers usually came from newly bought recruits, not sons.

The sultanate defeated the Mongols, expelled the last Crusaders (Acre, 1291), hosted figurehead Abbasid caliphs in Cairo and filled Cairo with mosques, madrasas and tombs. It fell to the Ottomans in 1516–1517.

Common confusion: Mamluks vs Janissaries. Both were slave-origin soldiers, but Mamluks were bought from outside the realm and became rulers; Janissaries were levied from Ottoman Christian subjects and served the sultan.
cards.example: At ‘Ayn Jalut (1260) in Palestine, the Mamluk army under Qutuz and Baybars defeated a Mongol force, halting the Mongol advance on Egypt.
numbers: Fall of Acre, last Crusader stronghold
cards.numbersSource: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Mamluk”, “Battle of ʿAyn Jālūt” and “Acre”.
played: 1250: mamluk officers seize power from the Ayyubids in Egypt.
1260: victory over the Mongols at ‘Ayn Jalut.
1261: a surviving Abbasid is installed as caliph in Cairo, lending legitimacy.
1516–1517: Ottoman Sultan Selim I conquers Syria and Egypt.

cards.simple: The Ottoman (c. 1299–1922), Safavid (1501–1736) and Mughal (1526–1857) empires: three large early modern Muslim states built on firearms, standing armies and centralized administration.
more: The label comes from the historians Marshall Hodgson and William McNeill: three large, long-lived states that used firearms and artillery, centralized bureaucracies and court-sponsored art. Many historians now treat it as a convenient grouping rather than an explanation.

They differed sharply. The Ottomans were Sunni (Hanafi) and ruled a multi-religious empire from the Balkans to Arabia. The Safavids grew out of a Sufi order and imposed Twelver Shi‘ism on Iran. The Mughals, descended from Timur and Chinggis Khan, ruled a mostly Hindu population; Akbar (r. 1556–1605) promoted tolerance.
Common confusion: “Ottoman” is not “Turkish” in the modern national sense, and Safavid Iran was not Shi‘i before 1501; most Iranians were then Sunni.
cards.example: At Chaldiran (1514) the Ottoman army, with artillery and Janissary musketeers, defeated the Safavid cavalry, fixing a frontier between Sunni Ottoman and Shi‘i Iranian lands.
played: 1453: Mehmed II takes Constantinople, which becomes Istanbul.
1501: Shah Isma‘il I founds the Safavid state at Tabriz.
1514: the Ottomans defeat the Safavids at Chaldiran; 1526: Babur wins at Panipat and founds the Mughal empire.
1598: Shah ‘Abbas I makes Isfahan the Safavid capital.

cards.simple: The Ottoman levy of Christian boys, converted and trained for the Janissary infantry or palace and state service.
more: Officials periodically took boys from Christian peasant families, mostly in the Balkans. The most promising were educated in the palace and could rise to the highest offices; the rest became Janissaries, the sultan’s salaried standing infantry, an early user of firearms.

Because they owed everything to the sultan, these “slaves of the Porte” were a counterweight to the landed cavalry and old families. The levy sat uneasily with the usual legal protection of dhimmis, and it faded in the 17th century as Janissary posts became hereditary and open to Muslims.
Common confusion: the devshirme is not the millet system and not the Mamluk institution. By the 18th century the Janissaries were a powerful, often rebellious corps; Mahmud II destroyed it in 1826.
cards.example: The architect Sinan (c. 1490–1588) entered Ottoman service through the devshirme, served as a Janissary engineer, and became chief architect, designing the Süleymaniye Mosque.
numbers: Sokollu Mehmed Pasha, devshirme recruit, grand vizier
played: A boy is taken from a Balkan village and sent to Anatolia to learn Turkish and Islam.
He is selected for the palace school or the Janissary corps.
Talent and loyalty bring promotion: governor, general, grand vizier.
1826: the Janissaries resist reform and are abolished by Mahmud II.

cards.simple: Ottoman arrangement in which religious communities (e.g. Greek Orthodox, Armenian, Jewish) ran their own personal-status law and internal affairs under their leaders.
more: Each community’s religious head was responsible to the state for its taxes and order. Within it, its own courts handled marriage, divorce and inheritance, and it ran its own churches, synagogues, schools and charities.

Historians such as Benjamin Braude argue that a formal, empire-wide “millet system” is largely a 19th-century creation; earlier arrangements were local and ad hoc, built on the older dhimmi framework. In the Tanzimat era communities received written constitutions, and “millet” shifted toward meaning “nation”.

Common confusion: the millet arrangement did not mean equality: non-Muslims kept dhimmi status until the reforms of 1839–1856. Its legacy survives in religious personal-status courts in Lebanon and Israel.
cards.example: After taking Constantinople in 1453, Mehmed II installed Gennadios Scholarios as Greek Orthodox Patriarch, responsible for the Orthodox community.
played: 1453: Mehmed II appoints a patriarch to lead the Orthodox.
Community courts settle a Jewish or Armenian family’s inheritance by their own law.
1856: the Reform Edict promises equality to all subjects.
1863: the Armenian National Constitution reorganizes that community with an elected assembly.

cards.simple: The classical Arabic ode: a long poem in one rhyme and meter that traditionally opens with a nostalgic prelude (nasib) at an abandoned campsite, then moves through a journey to a main theme such as praise.
more: Pre-Islamic poets perfected the form; the most famous odes were later gathered as the Mu‘allaqat (“suspended” poems). The critic Ibn Qutayba (d. 889) described the three-part scheme: nasib (lost love at the ruined camp), rahil (the desert journey) and the main purpose: praise (madih), boasting or satire.
Under the caliphs it became the court poem of praise. Poets in Persian, Turkish and Urdu adopted it, and religious qasidas praise the Prophet.
Common confusion: qasida vs ghazal. The qasida is long, public and often panegyric; the ghazal is a shorter love lyric that grew out of the qasida’s amatory opening.
cards.example: Imru’ al-Qays’s Mu‘allaqa opens “Stop, let us weep at the memory of a beloved and an abode”, the classic nasib at the deserted campsite.
played: Nasib: the poet halts at the traces of a deserted camp and remembers his beloved.
Rahil: he rides off across the desert, praising his camel’s endurance.
Madih: he arrives at the patron and praises his generosity and courage.
At Sayf al-Dawla’s court in Aleppo, al-Mutanabbi (915–965) made this form famous.

cards.simple: A short love lyric in monorhyme couplets, central to Persian poetry (Hafez), in which earthly and divine love often blur.
more: Arab poets of the Umayyad period made love poetry an independent form; Persian poets turned the ghazal into a tightly built lyric of about 5–15 couplets. The first couplet rhymes in both lines; afterwards only the second line of each couplet does, often followed by a repeated refrain (radif). The poet names himself in the last couplet (takhallus).

Its stock images, wine, the tavern, the cruel beloved, the nightingale and the rose, can be read as worldly or as Sufi symbols of divine love and intoxication with God. The ambiguity is part of the art.
Common confusion: ghazal vs ruba‘i (a single quatrain, as in Omar Khayyam) vs masnavi (long narrative poetry in rhyming couplets, as in Rumi’s Masnavi).
cards.example: The Divan of Hafez (c. 1325–1390) of Shiraz: Iranians still open it at random to read their fortune (fal-e Hafez).
played: Couplet 1 sets the rhyme and refrain in both lines.
Each later couplet is a self-contained image, linked by rhyme and mood rather than story.
Wine and the beloved can be read literally or mystically.
The last couplet names the poet, often addressing himself.

cards.simple: Refined culture and etiquette, and the literature of the cultivated person: anthologies, belles-lettres, wit and moral instruction.
more: Adab was the knowledge expected of a cultured courtier or secretary (katib): poetry, history, proverbs, anecdotes and good manners. It drew on Arabic, Persian and Greek sources and was meant to delight and instruct.

Masters include al-Jahiz of Basra (d. 868/869), essayist on everything from animals to misers, and Ibn al-Muqaffa‘ (8th c.), who translated Kalila wa-Dimna from Middle Persian. In modern Arabic, adab simply means “literature”.
Common confusion: adab is not religious law or ritual etiquette alone; it is a secular-leaning humanistic culture that coexisted with religious learning.
cards.example: Kalila wa-Dimna, animal fables of Indian origin about the conduct of kings, passed through Middle Persian into Arabic and then into many languages.
played: A young secretary memorizes poetry, proverbs and model letters.
He reads anthologies like Ibn Qutayba’s ‘Uyun al-akhbar (“Choice Reports”).
Later he enjoys al-Hariri’s Maqamat (early 12th c.), virtuoso tales of a silver-tongued rogue.
A 1237 manuscript of the Maqamat illustrated by al-Wasiti shows how adab and painting met.

cards.simple: Honeycomb or “stalactite” vaulting built from tiers of small niches, used in domes, portals and transitions, as in the Alhambra.
more: Muqarnas appears from about the 10th–11th centuries, in Iran and Iraq and in North Africa. Each tier of small niches projects over the one below, so it can turn a square corner into the round base of a dome, or fill a portal’s half-dome.

It is often non-structural: carved in stone, or hung in plaster or wood beneath the real roof. Built from a small set of repeated units, it spread across the Islamic world and beyond, to the 1140s ceiling of the Cappella Palatina in Norman Palermo.
Common confusion: muqarnas is three-dimensional vaulting; arabesque is flat ornament. A mihrab may contain muqarnas, but it is a different thing.
cards.example: The ceiling of the Hall of the Abencerrajes in the Alhambra, Granada (14th c., Nasrid), an eight-pointed star of thousands of muqarnas cells.
played: A square hall needs a round dome.
At the corners, a first row of small niches steps out.
Each higher tier projects further, closing the gap.
The top tier forms the circle on which the dome rests.

cards.simple: Infinitely extendable patterns of scrolling, interlacing vegetal forms, alongside geometric patterns and calligraphy in Islamic ornament.
more: “Arabesque” is a European term; in Persian and Turkish the vegetal scroll is called islimi. Stems split and rejoin so that the pattern has no natural end, suited to covering whole surfaces of stucco, tile, wood and manuscripts.

Islamic ornament combines three systems: vegetal (arabesque), geometric (star and polygon patterns) and calligraphic (Qur’anic and poetic inscriptions). Religious buildings generally avoid images of people and animals.

Common confusion: “Islam forbids all images” is too simple. Figurative painting flourished in palaces and illustrated books, such as Persian and Mughal miniatures; the avoidance applies mainly to religious spaces.
cards.example: The mosaics of the Dome of the Rock (691–692) show scrolling vines, trees and jewelled vessels with no human or animal figures.
played: Start from a single stem.
It splits into a leaf and a new stem, which curls back.
The new stem splits again, interlacing with the first.
Repeated across a wall, the pattern runs on without end.

cards.simple: The key parts of a mosque: the mihrab (niche marking the qibla, the direction of Mecca), the minbar (pulpit for the Friday sermon), the minaret (tower for the call to prayer) and, in Iranian plans, the iwan (vaulted hall open on one side).
more: Prayer is performed in rows facing the qibla, so congregational mosques are often broad rather than deep. The first mosque was the courtyard of the Prophet’s house in Medina; the concave mihrab became standard from the Umayyad period.
Regional plans differ: the Arab hypostyle hall with a courtyard (Córdoba), the Iranian four-iwan courtyard plan (Isfahan) and the Ottoman central-dome plan (Sinan’s Istanbul mosques).
Common confusion: the mihrab is not an altar and nothing is offered there; it only marks direction. The imam leads prayer near it, but preaches from the minbar.
cards.example: In the Great Mosque of Córdoba, begun c. 785, a forest of double arches leads to the 10th-century mihrab of al-Hakam II, decorated with Byzantine-style gold mosaics.
cards.numbersSource: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Mosque-Cathedral of Córdoba” and “Süleymaniye Mosque” (sources give the dome as 26–27 m across).
played: Enter the courtyard and wash at the ablution fountain.
Inside, stand in rows parallel to the qibla wall.
The imam leads the prayer from in front of the mihrab.
On Friday he preaches the sermon (khutba) from the minbar.

cards.simple: Ottoman reform era: centralization, legal equality of subjects regardless of religion, new courts, schools and codes on European models.
more: Statesmen such as Mustafa Reşid Pasha sought to save the empire from European pressure and internal revolt by strengthening the central state. The Gülhane edict of 1839 promised security of life and property and fair taxation; the Reform Edict of 1856 declared Muslims and non-Muslims equal.
New secular courts, schools and codes followed. The era closed with the first Ottoman constitution (1876), which Abdülhamid II suspended in 1878.
Common confusion: the Tanzimat is not the Young Turk revolution (1908), and not simple Westernization: the Mecelle civil code (1869–1876) codified Hanafi law in modern form.
cards.example: The Mecelle, drafted by a commission under Ahmed Cevdet Pasha, codified Islamic civil law in numbered articles like a European code; parts stayed in force in some successor states for decades.
played: 1826: the Janissaries are abolished, clearing the way for a new army.
1839: the Gülhane edict opens the Tanzimat.
1856: the Reform Edict declares legal equality and ends the jizya.
1876: a constitution and parliament; suspended two years later.

cards.simple: The Arab “awakening/renaissance” of the 19th and early 20th centuries: printing, journalism, translation, new literary forms and the revival of classical Arabic.
more: Centred on Cairo and Beirut, it was carried by Muslim and Christian intellectuals alike: the government press at Bulaq, Muhammad ‘Ali’s educational missions to Europe, Butrus al-Bustani’s encyclopaedia and dictionary, and dozens of journals.

Writers revived classical Arabic style while adopting new forms (the novel, drama, the newspaper essay), and debated how to be modern without simply copying Europe. It fed both Islamic modernism and Arab nationalism.
Common confusion: the Nahda is cultural and literary; the Tanzimat is Ottoman state reform. Historians also now question the old story of a long “decline” before the Nahda.
cards.example: Rifa‘a al-Tahtawi (1801–1873), imam to an Egyptian student mission in Paris (1826–1831), described French society and institutions in Takhlis al-ibriz (1834).
played: 1798: Napoleon’s invasion of Egypt shocks Ottoman Arab elites.
1820s: Muhammad ‘Ali founds the Bulaq press and sends students to Europe.
Later 19th century: journals and translations multiply in Beirut and Cairo.
1988: Naguib Mahfouz (1911–2006), heir to the modern Arabic novel, wins the Nobel Prize.

cards.simple: Late 19th-century reform movement (al-Afghani, Muhammad ‘Abduh) arguing that Islam is compatible with reason, science and modern institutions.
more: Modernists argued that Muslims had fallen behind not because of Islam but because of blind imitation (taqlid) of past jurists. They called for renewed ijtihad, modern education and a return to the faith’s original sources as they read them.

Jamal al-Din al-Afghani (1838/39–1897) preached pan-Islamic unity against European imperialism. His disciple Muhammad ‘Abduh (1849–1905), Grand Mufti of Egypt from 1899, pursued legal and educational reform; Rashid Rida carried the project on in the journal al-Manar. In India, Sayyid Ahmad Khan founded the Aligarh college (1875).
Common confusion: modernism is neither secularism nor later Islamism, though both drew on it. Rida’s later thought moved toward more conservative Salafi positions.
cards.example: ‘Abduh’s Theology of Unity (Risalat al-tawhid) argued that reason and revelation cannot truly conflict.
played: Problem: European military, economic and colonial dominance.
Diagnosis: not Islam, but taqlid and neglect of reason.
Remedy: ijtihad, science and reformed education, judged by the Qur’an and sunna.
Result: reforms at al-Azhar and in law; later movements claim the legacy in different directions.

cards.simple: A secret Anglo-French agreement of 1916 dividing the Ottoman Arab lands into spheres of influence, which remains a symbol of colonial borders in the Middle East.
more: Negotiated by Mark Sykes and François Georges-Picot in 1916, it gave France a sphere in Syria and Lebanon and Britain one in Iraq and toward the Gulf, with Palestine to be international. It conflicted with British promises to Sharif Husayn of Mecca (the Husayn–McMahon correspondence) and with the Balfour Declaration (1917).
After the war the San Remo conference (1920) assigned League of Nations mandates: Syria and Lebanon to France; Iraq, Palestine and Transjordan to Britain.

Common confusion: Sykes–Picot did not itself draw today’s borders; those came from later postwar settlements. It endures as a symbol of Western betrayal because it was secret and revealed by the Bolsheviks in 1917.
cards.example: The French Mandate for Syria and Lebanon (from 1920), with the separate state of Greater Lebanon proclaimed in 1920.
cards.numbersSource: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Sykes-Picot Agreement” and “San Remo Conference”.
played: 1915–1916: Britain courts Sharif Husayn with promises of Arab independence.
1916: Britain and France secretly divide the region in the Sykes–Picot agreement.
1917: the Bolsheviks publish the secret treaty.
1920: San Remo assigns the mandates; 1924: the caliphate is abolished.

cards.simple: Edward Said’s argument that Western scholarship, art and literature constructed “the Orient” as an exotic, inferior Other, a body of knowledge entangled with imperial power.
more: Drawing on Michel Foucault’s idea of discourse, Edward Said (1935–2003) argued that European writers, travellers, painters and scholars produced a stable image of an unchanging, irrational, sensual East that justified rule over it. Knowledge and power reinforced each other.

The book helped found postcolonial studies. Critics such as Bernard Lewis and Robert Irwin defended the scholarly tradition; Sadik al-Azm warned of an “Orientalism in reverse” that essentializes the West.
Common confusion: “Orientalism” has three senses: the academic study of Asian languages and cultures, a 19th-century style of painting, and Said’s critical sense of a discourse of power.
cards.example: Jean-Léon Gérôme’s painting The Snake Charmer (c. 1879), a timeless, exotic East, appears on the cover of a widely sold edition of Orientalism.
played: A European traveller writes that “the Oriental” is timeless and irrational.
Scholars and novelists repeat the image; it becomes common knowledge.
Administrators cite that knowledge to justify colonial rule.
Said (1978) shows the circle, and asks who has the power to represent whom.

questions.label: Q1
questions.prompt: An 11th-century Baghdad merchant permanently dedicates the rent from his shops to pay teachers at a new school. What legal instrument is he using?

options.why: A perpetual charitable endowment: the shops can never be sold, and their income goes to the purpose in the deed. Waqfs typically funded madrasas, mosques and hospitals.
Confuses a voluntary, permanent endowment with the obligatory annual alms on wealth (one of the five pillars). Zakat is paid out each year; it doesn’t lock property away forever.
Confuses giving with taxation: the jizya was the poll tax non-Muslim dhimmis paid to the state, not a gift a Muslim makes to a school.
Confuses a legal opinion with a legal instrument. A mufti might issue a fatwa about a waqf, but a fatwa itself transfers no property.

questions.pattern: Waqf = permanent + income + named purpose. If property is taken off the market for good and only its income is spent, on a school, mosque, hospital or family, it’s a waqf. Zakat is an annual duty; jizya is a tax; a fatwa is an opinion.
steps: Note the key word: permanently. That rules out a yearly payment like zakat.
The rent (income), not the shops themselves, goes to the teachers: an endowment.
No state is collecting anything, so it isn’t a tax (jizya).
Answer: waqf, the usual way madrasas like the Nizamiyya were funded.

questions.label: Q2
questions.prompt: A jurist works out whether a new kind of contract is permitted by reasoning from the Qur’an, hadith, scholarly consensus and analogy. This activity is…

options.why: Jurisprudence: the human effort to derive rulings from the sources of law. Consensus (ijma‘) and analogy (qiyas) are among its sources.
Confuses law with theology. Kalam argues about doctrine (God’s attributes, free will, whether the Qur’an is created), not whether a contract is permitted.
Confuses legal reasoning with philosophy in the Greek tradition. Falsafa starts from Aristotle and demonstration, not from Qur’an, hadith, ijma‘ and qiyas.
Confuses one input with the whole process. Tafsir is Qur’an commentary; a jurist may use it, but deriving a ruling from all four sources is fiqh.

questions.pattern: The four sources (Qur’an → sunna → ijma‘ → qiyas) + a question about what’s allowed = fiqh. Sharia is the ideal law; fiqh is the human reasoning toward it. Kalam = theology, falsafa = philosophy, tafsir = commentary.
steps: The question is practical: is this act (a contract) permitted? That’s a legal ruling.
The sources named are exactly the classical sources of law (usul al-fiqh).
Theology (kalam) and philosophy (falsafa) answer different questions.
Answer: fiqh; the effort itself is called ijtihad.

questions.label: Q3
questions.prompt: An octagonal shrine with a gilded dome over a rock outcrop in Jerusalem, built under the Umayyad caliph ‘Abd al-Malik around 691–692.

options.why: The earliest major surviving Islamic monument, a domed shrine rather than a congregational mosque.
Mixes up the two buildings on the same platform: al-Aqsa is the nearby congregational mosque, rectangular in plan, not the octagonal domed shrine.
Right dynasty, wrong city and ruler: also Umayyad, but in Damascus and built under al-Walid I in the early 8th century.
Wrong century and empire: a 6th-century Byzantine church in Constantinople, converted to a mosque only in 1453.

questions.pattern: Identify a monument by place + date + patron + plan. Jerusalem + ‘Abd al-Malik + 691–692 + octagon over a rock = Dome of the Rock. Al-Aqsa shares the site but is a rectangular mosque.
steps: Place: Jerusalem rules out Damascus and Constantinople.
Plan: octagonal and domed, a shrine, not a hall for rows of worshippers.
Date and patron: ‘Abd al-Malik, 691–692 (72 AH).
Answer: the Dome of the Rock.

questions.label: Q4
questions.prompt: Tiers of small, stacked niches forming a honeycomb-like vault, famous in the Alhambra’s halls.

options.why: The “stalactite” vaulting typical of Islamic architecture from the 11th–12th c. on.
Confuses flat ornament with 3-D vaulting: arabesque is scrolling vegetal pattern on a surface, not stacked niches.
Confuses a whole space with its decoration: an iwan is a single large vaulted hall open on one side (it may contain muqarnas).
Confuses function with form: the mihrab is the niche showing the direction of prayer. It can contain muqarnas, but it’s a different thing.

questions.pattern: Muqarnas = many small niches in projecting tiers (3-D). Arabesque = flat vegetal scroll. Iwan = one big open vault. Mihrab = the qibla niche.
steps: “Tiers of small, stacked niches” is three-dimensional, so not arabesque.
Many small niches, not one big vaulted hall, so not an iwan.
It’s a vaulting technique, not a liturgical feature, so not the mihrab.
Answer: muqarnas, as in the Hall of the Abencerrajes.

questions.label: Q5
questions.prompt: A Safavid mosque in Isfahan’s great square with no minaret and no courtyard, built for the royal household (early 17th c.).

options.why: Its unusual plan, a single domed chamber, reflects its use as a private royal mosque.
Right square, wrong building: the Shah Mosque is the great congregational mosque on the same square, with minarets, four iwans and a courtyard.
Mixes up Safavid and Ottoman: the Blue Mosque is in Istanbul and has six minarets, the opposite of “no minaret”.
Mixes up Safavid and Mughal, and a tomb with a mosque: the Taj Mahal is a mausoleum in Agra.

questions.pattern: Use the clues that exclude. Isfahan = Safavid (not Ottoman Istanbul, not Mughal Agra). “No minaret, no courtyard” excludes a congregational mosque like the Shah Mosque, leaving the private royal mosque.
steps: Isfahan’s square (Naqsh-e Jahan) belongs to Shah ‘Abbas I’s capital: Safavid.
That rules out the Ottoman Blue Mosque and the Mughal Taj Mahal.
A congregational mosque needs a courtyard; the Shah Mosque has one.
Answer: Sheikh Lotfollah, a domed chamber for the court.

questions.label: Q6
questions.prompt: An early 17th-century Ottoman mosque in Istanbul, unusual for having six minarets.

options.why: Built 1609–1616 for Sultan Ahmed I. Its blue İznik tiles gave the nickname.
Right city, wrong date: Sinan’s masterpiece of 1550–1557 for Süleyman, with four minarets.
Right architect’s era, wrong city: Sinan’s late masterpiece is in Edirne (1570s), with four minarets.
Confuses a converted church with a purpose-built mosque: its minarets were added after 1453, and there are four.

questions.pattern: Match the Ottoman imperial mosques by date and minarets. Süleymaniye 1550–1557 (4), Selimiye in Edirne 1570s (4), Sultan Ahmed 1609–1616 (6).
steps: Early 17th century rules out Sinan’s 16th-century mosques.
Six minarets is the distinctive clue.
Hagia Sophia was a church until 1453 and has four.
Answer: the Sultan Ahmed (Blue) Mosque.

questions.label: Q7
questions.prompt: Ibn Khaldun explains the rise and fall of dynasties through a group’s cohesion, which is strong among desert peoples and weakened by luxury. He calls it…

options.why: Group solidarity, the engine of his cyclical theory in the Muqaddima (1377).
Confuses the whole community of believers, bound by faith, with the tribal or group solidarity that wins power and then fades.
Confuses a source of law with a social force: ijma‘ is the consensus of scholars.
Confuses spiritual power with political cohesion: baraka is blessing, often linked to saints and Sufi masters.

questions.pattern: Ibn Khaldun’s cycle: a group with strong ‘asabiyya conquers, founds a dynasty, settles into luxury, loses cohesion and is replaced by a tougher group, typically within about three generations.
steps: The question asks for a social force that rises and decays.
Umma is religious community; ijma‘ is legal consensus; baraka is blessing.
Ibn Khaldun (1332–1406) named group solidarity ‘asabiyya.
Answer: ‘asabiyya.

questions.label: Q8

options.t: The Mongols sacked Baghdad, ending the Abbasid caliphate there
options.why: Hülegü’s army took the city and killed the caliph al-Musta‘sim.
Off by two centuries: that was 1453, under Mehmed II.
Confuses the end of the Abbasids with an early Umayyad event: Karbala was 680.

options.t: Granada fell to Castile and Aragon
options.why: Confuses the end of the Abbasids in the east with the end of Muslim rule in Iberia, 1492.

questions.pattern: Anchor dates for dynasties: 661 Umayyads, 750 Abbasids, 1258 Mongols take Baghdad, 1260 ‘Ayn Jalut, 1453 Constantinople, 1492 Granada, 1517 Ottomans take Egypt.
steps: 1258 sits in the middle period, after the Seljuks and Crusades.
Karbala (680) is far too early; 1453 and 1492 are far too late.
The Mongols under Hülegü took Baghdad and executed the caliph.
Two years later the Mamluks stopped them at ‘Ayn Jalut (1260).

questions.label: Q9
questions.prompt: The Sunni–Shi‘i divide began as a disagreement about…

options.t: Who should lead the community after Muhammad
options.why: Shi‘is backed ‘Ali and his descendants. Theological and legal differences grew later.
Projects a difference that isn’t there: Sunnis and Shi‘is share the same Qur’an.
Both pray toward Mecca; the qibla is shared, as are the five pillars.
Confuses a later, cross-cutting movement with the origin: Sufism exists in both traditions and isn’t the source of the split.

questions.pattern: Origin vs later development. The divide began over leadership (‘Ali and his line vs the community’s choice of caliph). Distinct theology, law (the Ja‘fari school) and ritual came later; scripture and pillars are shared.
steps: Ask what was at stake in 632: who leads now that Muhammad has died?
Sunnis accept the four caliphs in order; Shi‘is hold ‘Ali was designated.
Karbala (680) turned the dispute into a lasting religious identity.
Answer: leadership after Muhammad.

questions.label: Q10
questions.prompt: The Ottoman practice of levying Christian boys to be converted and trained for the Janissaries and state service is called…

options.why: The “collection”: boys from Christian subjects, mostly in the Balkans, trained for the palace or the Janissary corps.
Confuses Ottoman policies toward non-Muslims: the millets were self-governing religious communities, not a levy of boys.
Confuses two ways of paying for an army: a timar was a land-revenue grant supporting a cavalryman, while the Janissaries were salaried infantry.
Wrong era: the Tanzimat was the 19th-century reform programme, which followed the Janissaries’ abolition in 1826.

questions.pattern: Ottoman terms by function: devshirme = recruiting (boys → Janissaries, officials); timar = paying cavalry with land revenue; millet = governing religious communities; Tanzimat = 19th-c. reform.
steps: The question is about recruitment of soldiers and officials.
Millet (communities) and Tanzimat (reforms) are different institutions.
Timar pays cavalry; it doesn’t recruit boys.
Answer: devshirme.

questions.label: Q11
questions.prompt: A short monorhyme love lyric, in which earthly and divine love often blur, perfected in Persian by Hafez.

options.why: Hafez’s Divan is the classic collection of ghazals.
Confuses length and purpose: the qasida is the longer, multi-part ode, often praising a patron.
Confuses forms by line count: a ruba‘i is a single quatrain (four lines), the form of Omar Khayyam’s Rubaiyat.
Confuses lyric with narrative: a masnavi is long narrative or didactic poetry in rhyming couplets, like Rumi’s Masnavi.

questions.pattern: Persian/Arabic verse forms: qasida = long ode (praise); ghazal = short love lyric, one rhyme; ruba‘i = one quatrain; masnavi = long poem in rhyming couplets.
steps: “Short” rules out the qasida and the masnavi.
“Love lyric” in many couplets, not a single four-line epigram, rules out the ruba‘i.
Hafez (c. 1325–1390) is the master of the form.
Answer: ghazal.

questions.label: Q12

options.t: Western representations of “the Orient” constructed it as an inferior Other, entangled with imperial power
options.why: Knowledge and power reinforce each other.

options.t: Middle Eastern societies were unchanged for centuries
options.why: Reverses his argument: the image of a timeless, unchanging East is exactly what Said criticizes.

options.t: Orientalist painters were the most accurate observers of the Middle East
options.why: Reverses his argument: he treats such images as projections of European fantasy, not documents.

options.t: The Ottoman Empire collapsed because of Sufism
options.why: Not his subject: the book is about Western representation, not Ottoman history or religion.

questions.pattern: Said’s thesis in one line: the West’s knowledge of “the Orient” was a discourse that made the East exotic and inferior and served imperial rule.
steps: Said studies Western texts and images, not Middle Eastern history itself.
Options claiming the East was timeless or accurately painted are the views he attacks.
His key move links knowledge to power (after Foucault).
Answer: the first option.

questions.label: Q13
questions.prompt: Year 1 of the Islamic (AH) calendar corresponds to…

options.why: The calendar counts from the emigration, the founding of the community.
Assumes the calendar works like AD (counting from a birth); it counts from the hijra instead.
Confuses the start of the Qur’an’s revelation with the start of the community: an important date, but not the calendar’s start.
Confuses the start of the caliphate with the start of the calendar.

questions.pattern: AH = “in the year of the hijra”. Year 1 begins in 622, when the community was founded at Medina. Islamic years are lunar (≈ 354 days), so they don’t line up with CE years.
steps: Order the founding dates: 570 birth, 610 revelation, 622 hijra, 632 death.
The calendar marks the community, not the person or the revelation.
So 1 AH = 622 CE.
Being lunar, AH years run faster: Ramadan moves about 11 days earlier each year.

questions.label: Q14
questions.prompt: The 19th-century Arab literary and cultural revival of printing, journalism and new literary forms is called…

options.why: “Awakening” or “renaissance”, centred on Cairo and Beirut.
Confuses cultural revival with state reform: the Tanzimat was the Ottoman government’s reorganization (1839–1876).
Wrong era entirely: the Jahiliyya is the pre-Islamic “age of ignorance” in Muslim tradition.
Wrong place and era: the Reconquista was the Christian conquest of al-Andalus, completed in 1492.

questions.pattern: Two 19th-century currents: Nahda = Arab cultural and literary revival (presses, journals, the novel); Tanzimat = Ottoman state reform (edicts, courts, codes).
steps: “Literary and cultural” points away from state reform (Tanzimat).
Jahiliyya and Reconquista are centuries off.
Printing presses (Bulaq), journals and translation define the movement.
Answer: the Nahda.
